136: Audit the score before explaining the rank
Align queries → understand the metric → check task coverage → distinguish score replay from training.

A cutoff is the instant at which a prediction is made. A checkpoint stores a fitted model’s state. Validation chooses that state; test measures the frozen choice. A seed controls a run’s random choices, not which database it tests.
Keep the aligned query keys from your leaderboard audit. Lesson 137 uses them to locate errors that the overall mean hides.
137: From a score to a diagnosis
Pair errors → define slices → count independent entities → propose a falsifiable repair.

A slice is a named subset of prediction queries. Support means how many queries and distinct entities it contains. A confidence interval here comes from a declared resampling procedure; it is not a guarantee about a new database.
Take your diagnosis checklist into Amazon: before explaining an error, establish what the task’s label actually observes.
138: From diagnosis to the meaning of a label
Build one eligible query → trace book-to-customer information → interpret the ranking → inspect reproduction evidence.

A graph node represents a database row. A message is a numerical contribution from a linked row. Two layers allow information to cross two edges. A positive label is the outcome coded as 1; here it means no future review, not a recorded purchase cancellation.
Carry the population check into the trial task: an absent future observation can mean no query, rather than label zero.
139: Transfer the pipeline, rebuild the question
Define the study population → trace a facility-to-study path → change the documented recipe → score keyed predictions.

A root is the study being predicted. Fanout limits how many neighbors are sampled per relation and hop. B is the number of queries in a batch; [B,128] means 128 learned coordinates for each query. BCE means binary cross-entropy, the training penalty for incorrect binary predictions. AUROC measures positive–negative ranking, with half credit for ties.
Keep both domain contracts. Lesson 140 asks you to defend complete runs, numerical closeness and protocol evidence as separate verdicts.
140: A checkpoint in reasoning, not just in training
Freeze the two recipes → select using validation → align keys → defend three separate verdicts.

A hyperparameter is a setting chosen outside gradient updates, such as learning rate or neighbor fanout. A percentage point is an absolute difference between percentages: 70% to 71% is one point. Sample SD describes spread among runs; it does not measure uncertainty across databases.
The next lesson changes the message itself. Use this checkpoint’s fixed-contract discipline to distinguish a new mechanism from evidence that it helps.
141: Draw one route → fuse source and fact → let the destination weight messages → trace the full model → inspect the evidence.

A tensor is an array with named dimensions. A channel is one coordinate of a learned vector. A linear map multiplies a vector by learned weights, optionally adding an offset. Neighbor sampling selects the rows available to the computation; model layers decide how those rows exchange information.
Keep the scalar source–fact–destination example. Lesson 142 uses controlled input changes to show exactly what an ordinary update can mix or repeat.
142: Explain the failure before claiming the fix
Count two-layer walks → construct a collision → compare the real networks → limit the conclusion.

A synchronous layer reads every node’s old state before producing new states. A collision means different inputs become the same representation. It matters for prediction only when their targets differ. A controlled scalar example can establish this mechanism without establishing its importance in a trained benchmark.
Carry both the mechanism and its limits into Lesson 143: reproducing a model requires checking feature meaning, training history and query identity as well as the score.
143: Turn a runnable model into an auditable claim
Freeze the recipe → verify feature meaning → inspect the forward pass → select a checkpoint → reconcile all runs.

MAE is the average absolute prediction error; lower is better. L1 loss uses those absolute errors for training. A gradient tells the optimizer how a parameter affects loss. NaN means “not a number”; finite predictions can coexist with invalid gradients. A differential oracle is an independent implementation run on the same inputs to compare outputs.
After predicting one number per driver, move to ranking many sponsors per facility. Lesson 144 asks how the candidate’s representation can depend on the query.
144: From one target to a ranked candidate set
Understand two towers → trace the local and distant branches → replace owner-specific scores → evaluate the full catalog.

A bipartite prediction problem links two entity roles, here facilities and sponsors. A dot product multiplies corresponding vector coordinates and sums them. B × N means a score for every one of B queries against every one of N candidates. “Local” means present in this query’s sampled graph, not geographically nearby.
ContextGNN changes how query–candidate scores are formed. Lesson 145 returns to a scalar target and changes communication among sampled rows with RelGT.
145: From contextual scores to contextual row tokens
Build five row descriptions → follow local and global attention → audit token ownership → interpret the reproduction boundary.

A token is one sampled row occurrence represented as a vector. A projection is a learned mapping to another vector space. Local attention compares tokens belonging to the same query. Global attention here reads a stored centroid memory; it does not fetch every database row at prediction time.
Use the access and selection audits in Lesson 146. A GNN–transformer comparison is meaningful only after specifying what each model saw and how its result was chosen.
146: From architecture diagrams to a fair comparison
Separate sampling from propagation → freeze selection → trace both course variants → pair errors on identical queries.

Readout is the operation that turns node states into the final prediction. An MLP is a feed-forward stack of learned linear maps and nonlinearities. A centroid is a representative vector for a group; EMA updates retain some old state while adding new training information. Matching seed labels does not make two different programs consume identical random draws.
Turn the unresolved comparison into a research question in Lesson 147. Name a missing measurement before proposing a larger model.
147: From a comparison to an investigation
Locate the information boundary → recheck the evidence → rank feasible questions → write a falsifier.

A mechanism describes how an operation could affect a prediction. A falsifier is a result that would refute a specific explanation. Transfer means reusing learned weights across tasks or databases; training new weights on another database is a different claim.
Bring one hypothesis to Lesson 148 and state the smallest intervention that could test it, including everything that must remain fixed.
148: From a research question to a controlled intervention
Locate the changed component → preserve query ownership → calculate paired effects → derive their interaction.

An ablation removes or replaces a component and retrains under a declared recipe. A paired effect subtracts the full-model score from the changed-model score within a seed. An interaction asks whether two changes together have the sum of their separate effects. None of these automatically divides total performance into percentages of credit.
Use the same discipline in Lesson 149: a weakness identifies where a procedure loses, while an intervention tests an explanation of that loss.
149: From component effects to the limits of the thesis
Define the comparator and sign → read the published catalog → inspect the fresh F1 case → propose a falsifier.

Provenance means where a value came from: a paper figure, saved predictions or fresh training. A point estimate is one reported summary, without its uncertainty. A baseline is the comparison procedure; changing its output head or training recipe changes the comparison.
Lesson 150 is under construction. Keep your weakness catalog and proposed falsifier for that checkpoint; until it is ready, finish the written defense here.
